newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk establishment reels from rebel Kurd missiles.
newsitem.headline: Turk establishment reels from rebel Kurd missiles.

text.p: Two deadly missile strikes against Turkish helicopters over northern Iraq have threatened to rewrite the military and political rules of engagement in the army's 12-year battle with the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK).

The admission by the authorities last week that rebel SA-7 missiles -- not "technical faults" as originally claimed -- brought down the two choppers has rocked Turkey's elite armed forces and touched off a nasty round of finger-pointing.

It has also raised the spectre of a humiliating pull-back from direct confrontation with the PKK, reminiscent of the Soviet retreat from Afghanistan once U.S.-made Stinger missiles allowed the mujaheddin to deny the Russians control of the air.
"Are the Cougars Flying Coffins?" asked the daily Zaman, in a reference to the downed Franco-German Cougar transport.
Caught in the cross-fire are the underpinnings of an anti-insurgency campaign that has cost about $7-$8 billion a year since 1984 and has claimed more than 23,000 lives.
"It's a whole new ballgame," said one Western diplomat.

"Mobile missiles mean Turkish forces can no longer fly helicopter missions at will against PKK positions. Ask the Soviets what happens next," said the analyst, who earlier served in the former Soviet Union.
Publicly, the Turkish General Staff insists the downings of the helicopters, with the loss of 13 men, has had no effect on the month-long campaign against PKK units inside Iraq.
"Flights over northern Iraq are continuing," a spokeswoman for the armed forces told Reuters.
But officials close to the operation, as well as reports from the region, suggest all is not well in the skies over Iraq.

Security sources in eastern Turkey, nerve centre for the anti-PKK effort, say helicopter flights have been restricted to "safe zones", with resupply of forward units forced to rely on dangerous and time-consuming overland routes.

Kurdish-language Med TV, whose first reports of the missile strikes were eventually confirmed by the military, said air activity over northern Iraq was severely restricted. "Turkish helicopters have not flown there for...days," Med TV said.
The pro-PKK DEM Agency said rebels had wiped out one Turkish patrol, stripped of air cover, and were poised to hit others.

Iraqi opposition sources, in contact with the region, said up to 1,000 PKK fighters, armed with Soviet-era Grad surface-to-surface missiles, had used the respite to cross into Iraq's Hakurk region from neighbouring Iran.

The entire region has been closed to journalists since Turkish troops poured across the border on May 14 to oust the PKK from Iraqi bases. Independent confirmation of the two sides' claims and counter-claims is impossible.

The SA-7s have also cut a trail of destruction through the political and military establishment, threatening the consensus that traditionally unites all shades of the political spectrum against the PKK fight for self-rule in eastern Turkey.
The secularist top brass has accused the Islamist-led government of under-funding the Iraq operation, part of a multi-billon dollar annual allocation for anti-PKK activities.
The generals also slammed the foreign ministry, itself a bastion of secularism, for not preventing the PKK from getting hold of up to 60 Russian-made SA-7 missiles abroad.
A leading general said last week the army had warned diplomats five times since 1992 that the rebels were trying to get the missiles from Iran, Syria, Armenia, Greece and Cyprus.
The foreign ministry denies the charges.
Meanwhile, MPs from the ruling Islamist Welfare Party have used the helicopter debacle to turn the tables on a military establishment already hard at work undermining the government.

Welfare deputy Azmi Ates demanded the secularist-run defence ministry investigate the purchase of the Cougar transports, suggesting political favouritism had influenced the choice of what he said were "cumbersome" and "unmanoeuvrable" aircraft.
"Do you think that the tender had a role in the killing of our soldiers in the disaster and that both state security and soldiers' lives were worth nothing?" Ates said.
As the witch-hunt picks up speed, commentators say the authorities are playing straight into the rebels' hands.

"The separatist...PKK must really be rejoicing over the fact that it has not only shot down two Turkish military helicopters in Iraq but it has helped cause a domestic and international row," wrote Daily News editor Ilnur Cevik.
